idiom_name: monitor + wait set with a re-checked predicate loop
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep the guarded state, one lock and one wait set together in the object that owns the state. A guarded method acquires the lock, evaluates the predicate, and while it is false releases the lock and parks in the wait set, re-checking after every wake; once the predicate holds it performs the action and releases the lock on every exit path. The notifier mutates the state and signals the wait set inside the same critical section - state changed first, notification second - so a waiter cannot lose the transition. Bounded waits (timeout or deadline) and cancellation belong to the wait itself, and a caller that must not be delayed belongs on the balking or queue-based alternative instead. Use the runtime's condition variable, queue or channel wherever one exists rather than hand-rolling a flag plus a polling loop.
code_sketch:
def take():
    lock.acquire()
    while not available(state):        # guard: re-checked after every wake
        wait(condition, lock)          # atomically release + park
    item = remove(state)               # guarded action on consistent state
    lock.release()                     # released on every exit path
    return item

def put(item):
    lock.acquire()
    add(state, item)                   # change state first
    signal_all(condition)              # then wake the wait set
    lock.release()
pitfalls: An if-guard instead of a while-guard executes the guarded action on a spurious wake-up or on a signal meant for a different predicate.
Notifying before the state change (or outside the critical section) loses the wake-up and hangs the caller, because the predicate is the only memory of the transition.
Blocking without a timeout, cancellation path or fairness policy turns a delayed notification into an unrecoverable stall.
Hand-rolling the wait set over a structure that already ships one (queue, channel, condition) reproduces subtle signalling bugs for no benefit.

Notification while the waiter has not yet entered the wait set: the notifier calls signal before the waiter has executed the wait instruction, so the signal is lost and the waiter sleeps indefinitely (lost-wakeup race on the notification side).

Nested suspension deadlock: a thread holds lock A and calls a guarded method that waits on condition B; the notifier of B needs lock A to change the state, creating a circular wait. This deadlock is invisible in single-caller tests and appears only under concurrent load.

signalAll when a single signal would suffice: on a high-contention queue or a monitor with many waiters for different predicates, broadcast wakes all waiters who each re-acquire the lock, find the predicate false, and immediately wait again — a thundering herd that creates a lock convoy and destroys throughput.

Waiting while holding locks needed by the notifier: any lock acquired before the wait that the notification path requires creates a potential lock-order inversion. Keep the lock set minimal and document lock ordering contracts explicitly.

Unchecked timeout expiration treated as success: a timed wait that expires and returns normally is indistinguishable from a woken waiter unless the caller explicitly checks the predicate. Treating an expired wait as 'condition satisfied' silently proceeds on stale state.

Wrong move: hand-rolling the check-park-signal sequence around a shared flag so the notifier can run between the predicate test and the park -> the wake-up is lost and the caller sleeps forever; this exact defect shipped in Go's standard library, where a lost wake-up in database/sql's closingMutex deadlocked Rows.Next against a concurrent Rows.Close (golang/go#81043) -> mutate the state and signal inside one critical section, and prefer the library predicate-form wait that owns that ordering.

Wrong move: reading a return from wait as proof the guard holds (Hoare-style reasoning - the notifier signalled, so the predicate must still be true) -> POSIX, the JVM, .NET, Rust and Go all use Mesa-style wake-ups, so a third thread can take the lock and flip the state first, or wake the caller spuriously, and the guarded action runs on an unsatisfied state -> re-test the predicate in a loop, or hand the predicate to wait_while / await(predicate) / wait(lock, pred) so the library loops for you.

Wrong move: one wait set plus notify()/signal for waiters on different predicates (producers and consumers, or several independent guards) -> the single wake-up lands on a waiter whose predicate is still false, it re-parks, and the state change is never consumed, so the program hangs exactly when the pool or queue is busy -> give each predicate its own condition, as ArrayBlockingQueue splits notEmpty and notFull, or broadcast and pay the herd.
